If V = 0, the same empty-basis argument applies. Assume V is nonzero. Choose a basis B of V as a Q_l-vector space (finite if one uses the standard finite-dimensionality of etale cohomology of smooth projective varieties; otherwise a Hamel basis). The set B_bar = {b tensor 1 : b in B} is a Q_l_bar-basis of V_bar. Indeed, every element of V_bar is a finite sum of elementary tensors v_i tensor a_i; writing each v_i as a finite Q_l-linear combination of elements of B and collecting coefficients gives a finite Q_l_bar-linear combination of elements of B_bar. Conversely, if sum_{b in B'} c_b (b tensor 1) = 0 with B' finite and c_b in Q_l_bar, then the tensors b tensor c_b give a finite sum in V tensor Q_l_bar equal to zero; by the universal property of the tensor product (or by applying a Q_l-linear functional separating the basis vectors) all c_b are zero.

For every b in B, F_bar(b tensor 1) = F(b) tensor 1 = lambda b tensor 1 = lambda (b tensor 1). Hence the matrix of F_bar in the basis B_bar is diagonal, with every diagonal entry equal to lambda. A diagonal matrix is diagonalizable. Therefore F_bar is diagonalizable on V_bar, and consequently F is semisimple on V.

Since n was arbitrary, F is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) for every integer n >= 0.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\) and \(r\ge1\) be integers, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) and let \(X_r=X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m}}\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^{mr}}\). For \(n\ge0\), the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) if and only if the \(q^{mr}\)-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_r)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
proof:
We fix the following notation throughout. Put K = \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) and \(L = \mathbb F_{q^{mr}}\); then \(K \subset L \subset k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q\), \(L/K\) is finite of degree \(r\), and \(q^{mr} = (q^m)^r\). For an integer \(s\ge 1\) write \(\sigma_s : k \to k\), \(\sigma_s(c) = c^{q^s}\), for the \(q^s\)-power automorphism of \(k\). Note two elementary facts we use repeatedly:
(1) \(\sigma_{mr} = \sigma_m^{\,r}\) (composition of \(\sigma_m\) with itself \(r\) times), since \(c^{(q^m)^r} = c^{q^{mr}}\).
(2) \(\sigma_{mr}\) restricts to the identity on \(L\): the fixed field of \(x\mapsto x^{q^{mr}}\) on \(\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) is exactly \(\mathbb F_{q^{mr}} = L\). In particular \(\sigma_{mr}\) is a \(K\)-automorphism of \(k\) (as \(K\subset L\)), and \(\sigma_m\) is also a \(K\)-automorphism of \(k\).

**Step 1: A canonical \(k\)-isomorphism \(\theta : X_k \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } (X_r)_k\).**
By definition \(X_r = X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}K}\operatorname{Spec}L\) and \((X_r)_k = X_r\times_{\operatorname{Spec}L}\operatorname{Spec}k\), while \(X_k = X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}K}\operatorname{Spec}k\). Associativity of fibre products and the \(k\)-linear isomorphism \(L\otimes_L k \xrightarrow{\sim} k\) give a canonical isomorphism of \(k\)-schemes
\[ (X_r)_k \;=\; (X\times_K L)\times_L k \;\cong\; X\times_K (L\times_L k)\;\cong\; X\times_K k \;=\; X_k . \]
Let us write \(\theta : X_k \to (X_r)_k\) for the inverse of this composite, and check it explicitly on rings so that nothing is hidden. Cover \(X\) by affine opens \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) with \(A\) a \(K\)-algebra; then \(X_r|_{\operatorname{Spec}A} = \operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_K L)\) and \((X_r)_k| = \operatorname{Spec}\bigl((A\otimes_K L)\otimes_L k\bigr)\), while \(X_k| = \operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_K k)\). Define
\[ \psi : (A\otimes_K L)\otimes_L k \longrightarrow A\otimes_K k,\qquad (a\otimes\lambda)\otimes c \longmapsto a\otimes \lambda c, \]
\[ \varphi : A\otimes_K k \longrightarrow (A\otimes_K L)\otimes_L k,\qquad a\otimes c \longmapsto (a\otimes 1)\otimes c . \]
Well-definedness of \(\psi\): the map \((A\otimes_K L)\times k\to A\otimes_K k\), \(((a\otimes\lambda),c)\mapsto a\otimes\lambda c\), is \(L\)-bilinear because \(((a\otimes\lambda)\mu, c)\mapsto a\otimes\lambda\mu c\) and \(((a\otimes\lambda),\mu c)\mapsto a\otimes\lambda\mu c\) agree for \(\mu\in L\); hence it descends to \(\otimes_L\). Well-definedness of \(\varphi\): for \(\mu\in K\), \(\varphi(a\mu\otimes c) = (a\mu\otimes 1)\otimes c = (a\otimes\mu)\otimes c = (a\otimes 1)\otimes \mu c = \varphi(a\otimes\mu c)\), using \(L\)-balancing with \(\mu\in K\subset L\); so \(\varphi\) is well defined on \(A\otimes_K k\). Finally
\[ \psi\varphi(a\otimes c) = \psi((a\otimes 1)\otimes c) = a\otimes c, \qquad \varphi\psi((a\otimes\lambda)\otimes c) = \varphi(a\otimes\lambda c) = (a\otimes 1)\otimes \lambda c = (a\otimes\lambda)\otimes c, \]
so \(\psi\) and \(\varphi\) are mutually inverse. Both are \(k\)-linear (\(k\) acts on the last factor on each side, and \(\psi((a\otimes\lambda)\otimes c\cdot c')=a\otimes\lambda cc' = c\,\psi((a\otimes\lambda)\otimes c')\)), so the isomorphisms glue over the affine cover to an isomorphism of \(k\)-schemes; we set \(\theta^\# = \psi\), i.e. \(\theta : X_k \xrightarrow{\sim} (X_r)_k\).

**Step 2: The two Frobenius morphisms, and their intertwining by \(\theta\).**
The \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of \(X_k\) is the scheme endomorphism \(F_m := \mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_m\) of \(X_k = X\times_K\operatorname{Spec}k\) (well defined because \(\sigma_m\) is a \(K\)-automorphism of \(k\)). The \(q^{mr}\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of \((X_r)_k\) is \(F_{mr} := \mathrm{id}_{X_r}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_{mr}\) of \(X_r\times_L\operatorname{Spec}k\) (well defined because \(\sigma_{mr}\) fixes \(L\)). On the affine rings above,
\[ F_m^\#(a\otimes c) = a\otimes\sigma_m(c),\qquad F_{mr}^\#\bigl((a\otimes\lambda)\otimes c\bigr) = (a\otimes\lambda)\otimes\sigma_{mr}(c). \]
By (1), \(F_m^{\,\circ r} = \mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_m^{r} = \mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_{mr}\), and \((F_m^{\,\circ r})^\# = \mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma_{mr}\). We compute, for generators,
\[ \theta^\#\bigl(F_{mr}^\#((a\otimes\lambda)\otimes c)\bigr) = \theta^\#\bigl((a\otimes\lambda)\otimes\sigma_{mr}(c)\bigr) = a\otimes \lambda\,\sigma_{mr}(c), \]
\[ (F_m^{\,\circ r})^\#\bigl(\theta^\#((a\otimes\lambda)\otimes c)\bigr) = (\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma_{mr})(a\otimes\lambda c) = a\otimes \sigma_{mr}(\lambda)\,\sigma_{mr}(c) = a\otimes \lambda\,\sigma_{mr}(c), \]
where the last equality uses (2), \(\sigma_{mr}|_L = \mathrm{id}\). Hence
\[ \theta^\#\circ F_{mr}^\# \;=\; (F_m^{\,\circ r})^\#\circ\theta^\#, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad F_{mr}\circ\theta \;=\; \theta\circ F_m^{\,\circ r} \ \ \text{as morphisms } X_k\to (X_r)_k . \]

**Step 3: Transport of the operators on cohomology.**
Étale cohomology is contravariant, so pulling back the relation of Step 2 gives, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[ \theta^*\circ F_{mr}^* \;=\; (F_m^{\,\circ r})^*\circ\theta^* \;=\; \bigl(F_m^*\bigr)^{r}\circ\theta^* . \]
Thus the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism \(\theta^* : H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_r)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) conjugates the \(q^{mr}\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \(A := F_{mr}^*\) on the source to \(T^r\) on the target, where \(T := F_m^*\) is the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\):
\[ \theta^*\, A\, (\theta^*)^{-1} \;=\; T^r . \tag{3.1} \]

**Step 4: The ambient spaces and operators are legitimate.**
By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob applied to the proper \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-variety \(X\) (with \(q^m = p^{am}\) in the role of the prime power, \(K = \mathbb F_{q^m}\), and \(K=\mathbb Q_\ell\) with its natural Frobenius structure), \(V := H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); the same lemma applied to \(X_r\), which is proper over \(\mathbb F_{q^{mr}}\), gives finite-dimensionality of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_r)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) (this also follows from (3.1) since \(\theta^*\) is an isomorphism). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a, \(T = (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_m)^*\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphism of \(V\) (its inverse being the geometric Frobenius pullback), so \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\) and \(T^r\) is defined for our \(r\ge 1\); likewise \(A\in\mathrm{GL}(H^n((X_r)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell))\).

**Step 5: Conjugate operators have the same semisimplicity status.**
We record the elementary linear algebra used here. Let \(P : W\xrightarrow{\sim} V\) be an isomorphism of finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces and let \(S\in\mathrm{GL}(W)\), and put \(S' = PSP^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\). Extending scalars, \(P_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell} : W\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell \xrightarrow{\sim} V\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is an isomorphism intertwining \(S\) and \(S'\). If \(W\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell = \bigoplus_{\alpha} \ker(S-\alpha)^{\oplus} \) is a decomposition into eigenspaces of \(S\), then \(V\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell = \bigoplus_\alpha P(\ker(S-\alpha))\) is the corresponding eigenspace decomposition of \(S'\) (since \(S'Pv = PSv = \alpha Pv\)), so \(S'\) is diagonalizable; the converse holds as well because \(S = P^{-1}S'P\). Equivalently, \(S\) and \(S'\) have the same minimal polynomial, and diagonalizability over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is the condition that this polynomial be a product of distinct linear factors. Hence \(S\) is semisimple if and only if \(S'\) is semisimple (in the sense of diagonalizability over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), which by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5 is equivalent to semisimplicity over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)).

**Step 6: Conclusion.**
By (3.1) and Step 5, \(A\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_r)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) if and only if \(T^r\) is semisimple on \(V\), i.e. if and only if the base change of \(T^r\) to \(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is diagonalizable (eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5). By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_319 applied to the finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-space \(V\), the element \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\), and the integer \(r\ge 1\), the base change of \(T^r\) to \(V\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is diagonalizable if and only if the base change of \(T\) is diagonalizable, i.e. (again by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5) if and only if \(T\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Chaining these equivalences,
\[ \text{\(q^{mr}\)-power Frobenius semisimple on } H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_r)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \iff \text{\(q^m\)-power Frobenius semisimple on } H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), \]
which is exactly the required statement. (If \(V = 0\), both sides are trivially true, and lemma_319 applies verbatim to the zero space, so no separate case is needed.) This completes the proof.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(Y\subset X\) be a nonempty smooth ample Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and let \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) be the closed immersion. Then \(i^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(n\le d-2\) and injective for \(n=d-1\), and these maps are equivariant for the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius.
proof:
**Notation and the prime power $Q$.** Put $Q:=q^m=p^{am}$, so $\mathbb F_Q=\mathbb F_{q^m}$. Since $\mathbb F_q\subseteq\mathbb F_{q^m}\subseteq k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$ and $k/\mathbb F_q$ is algebraic, $k$ is also an algebraic closure of $\mathbb F_{q^m}$; we write $\sigma:k\to k$, $\sigma(c)=c^{Q}=c^{q^m}$, for the corresponding automorphism, which restricts to the identity on $\mathbb F_{q^m}$. The $Q$-power arithmetic Frobenius endomorphisms of $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ are $F_X:=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ and $F_Y:=(\mathrm{id}_{Y_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$. Both lemmas we invoke below are stated for an arbitrary prime power in place of $q$, so they apply verbatim with $Q$ (and $am$ in place of $a$) in that role; we shall use them with $\mathbb F_Q$ as the ground field and the $Q$-power Frobenius.

Let $j:U:=X\setminus Y\hookrightarrow X$ be the open immersion of the complement.

**Step 1: $Y$ has pure dimension $d-1$ and is a proper subset of $X$.** The morphism $X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m}$ is smooth of pure dimension $d$, hence $X$ is regular and catenary, and every local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is a regular local ring, in particular an integral domain, of dimension $d-\dim\overline{\{x\}}$. Since $Y\subset X$ is an effective Cartier divisor, its ideal sheaf is invertible and is locally generated by a non-zero-divisor $f\in\mathcal O_{X,x}$; as $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is a domain this just means $f\neq 0$. Let $Z$ be an irreducible component of $Y$ with generic point $\eta$. The scheme $Y$ is smooth over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ by hypothesis, hence regular, hence reduced; therefore $\mathcal O_{Y,\eta}$ is a field, i.e. $\dim\mathcal O_{Y,\eta}=0$. But $\mathcal O_{Y,\eta}=\mathcal O_{X,\eta}/(f)$, and $\mathcal O_{X,\eta}$ is a regular local ring (hence Cohen--Macaulay) in which $f$ is a non-zero-divisor, so $\dim\mathcal O_{X,\eta}/(f)=\dim\mathcal O_{X,\eta}-1$. Thus $\dim\mathcal O_{X,\eta}=1$, i.e. $\eta$ is a point of codimension $1$ in $X$, and by catenarity/equidimensionality $\dim Z=\dim\overline{\{\eta\}}=d-1$. Hence $Y$ is of pure dimension $d-1$. Since $d\ge 2$, every irreducible component of $Y$ has dimension $d-1<d=\dim X$, so $Y\neq X$; together with non-emptiness this gives $\varnothing\neq Y\subsetneq X$. Also, $Y$ is ample by hypothesis (the line bundle $\mathcal O_X(Y)$ is ample), so $Y$ is a nonempty effective **ample Cartier** divisor defined over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, smooth of pure dimension $d-1$.

**Step 2: Vanishing of the compactly supported cohomology of $U$ below the middle degree.** The variety $X$ is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d\ge2$ over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, and $\varnothing\neq Y\subsetneq X$ is a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor defined over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, smooth of pure dimension $d-1$, by Step 1. Applying Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_hc_vanishing_ample_complement with $q$ replaced by $Q=q^m$ gives
\[
H^t_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\qquad\text{for every integer }t<d .
\tag{1}
\]

**Step 3: The Frobenius-equivariant localization sequence.** We now apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_283, again with $Q$ in place of $q$. Its hypotheses are exactly what we have: $X$ is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d\ge 1$ over $\mathbb F_Q$, and $Y\subset X$ is an effective ample divisor defined over $\mathbb F_Q$ which is smooth of pure dimension $d-1$ (Step 1), with open immersion $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ and closed immersion $i:Y\hookrightarrow X$. The lemma yields a long exact sequence of finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces
\[
\cdots\to H^n_{c}(U_k)\longrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k)\xrightarrow{\;i^*\;}H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k)\longrightarrow H^{n+1}_{c}(U_k)\to\cdots
\tag{2}
\]
(where $H^*(-)$ abbreviates $H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(-,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $H^*_c(U_k)$ abbreviates $H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$), whose middle map **is** the pullback $i^*$ induced by the closed immersion, and in which every map commutes with the $Q$-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms of the four terms.

**Step 4: The isomorphism range $n\le d-2$.** Étale cohomology vanishes in negative degrees, so for $n<0$ both $H^n(X_k)$ and $H^n(Y_k)$ are $0$ and $i^*$ is trivially an isomorphism, equivariant for $F_X=F_Y=0$ on zero spaces. Let $0\le n\le d-2$. Then $n<d$ and $n+1\le d-1<d$, so by (1) both $H^n_c(U_k)=0$ and $H^{n+1}_c(U_k)=0$. The piece of (2)
\[
0=H^n_c(U_k)\longrightarrow H^n(X_k)\xrightarrow{\;i^*\;}H^n(Y_k)\longrightarrow H^{n+1}_c(U_k)=0
\]
is exact: injectivity of $i^*$ follows because $\ker(i^*)=\operatorname{im}(H^n_c(U_k)\to H^n(X_k))=0$, and surjectivity follows because $\operatorname{im}(i^*)=\ker(H^n(Y_k)\to H^{n+1}_c(U_k))=H^n(Y_k)$. Hence $i^*$ is an isomorphism for every $n\le d-2$.

**Step 5: Injectivity in degree $n=d-1$.** Here $d-1<d$, so $H^{d-1}_c(U_k)=0$ by (1), and exactness of
\[
H^{d-1}_c(U_k)=0\longrightarrow H^{d-1}(X_k)\xrightarrow{\;i^*\;}H^{d-1}(Y_k)
\]
gives $\ker(i^*)=0$. Thus $i^*$ is injective in degree $d-1$. (No statement is made for $n\ge d$; the lemma does not assert one.)

**Step 6: Equivariance.** Fix $n\ge 0$. The assertion that the middle map of (2) commutes with the $Q$-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms of $H^n(X_k)$ and $H^n(Y_k)$ is precisely the identity of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear maps
\[
i^*\circ F_{X,n}\;=\;F_{Y,n}\circ i^*\;:\;H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),
\]
with $F_{X,n}=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ and $F_{Y,n}=(\mathrm{id}_{Y_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}$. Concretely, this is functoriality of étale cohomology applied to the commutative square of $k$-schemes
\[
\begin{array}{rcl}
Y_k & \xrightarrow{\;i_k\;} & X_k\\
\big\downarrow{\mathrm{id}\times\sigma} && \big\downarrow{\mathrm{id}\times\sigma}\\
Y_k & \xrightarrow{\;i_k\;} & X_k ,
\end{array}
\]
which commutes because $i$ is defined over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ and $\sigma$ restricts to the identity on $\mathbb F_{q^m}$: the base change of the closed immersion $i$ along $\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$ identifies canonically with $i_k$ itself. Thus the maps proved to be isomorphisms (for $n\le d-2$) and the injective map (for $n=d-1$) are all $q^m$-power-Frobenius equivariant.

**Conclusion.** For every integer $n\le d-2$ the pullback $i^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is an isomorphism, for $n=d-1$ it is injective, and all these maps commute with the $q^m$-power arithmetic Frobenius. This is exactly the statement of the lemma.

statement: Let \(Q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_Q\). Let \(X\) be a proper \(\mathbb F_Q\)-scheme, let \(Y\subset X\) be a closed \(\mathbb F_Q\)-subscheme, and let \(U=X\setminus Y\) be isomorphic over \(\mathbb F_Q\) to a finite disjoint union of affine spaces. For \(r\ge0\) let \(n_r\) be the number of connected components of \(U\) isomorphic to \(\mathbb A^r_{\mathbb F_Q}\). Suppose that for every \(r\ge0\), \(H^{2r}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(H^{2r}_{\acute et}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) are finite-dimensional, \(H^{2r+1}_{\acute et}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\), and the \(Q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius on \(H^{2r}_{\acute et}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) has characteristic polynomial \(P_r(T)\). Then, for every \(r\ge0\), the \(Q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius on \(H^{2r}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) has characteristic polynomial \(P_r(T)(T-Q^r)^{n_r}\).
proof:
Write Q=p^a, k=\overline{\mathbb F}_Q, \sigma(c)=c^Q, and for an \mathbb F_Q-scheme Z write Z_k=Z\times_{\mathbb F_Q}k and F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^* for the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius pullback. All cohomology groups below are \acute etale cohomology of the base-changed k-schemes with \mathbb Q_\ell coefficients; we abbreviate H^m(Z)=H^m_{\acute et}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). Fix the closed \mathbb F_Q-subscheme i:Y\hookrightarrow X and the open complement j:U=X\setminus Y; after base change we again write i:Y_k\hookrightarrow X_k and j:U_k\hookrightarrow X_k.

STEP 1 (the localisation long exact sequence). Since X is proper over \mathbb F_Q it is of finite type, hence X_k is of finite type over the algebraically closed field k, and i:Y_k\to X_k is a closed immersion with complementary open immersion j:U_k\to X_k. As \ell\neq p=\mathrm{char}(k), Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_localization_les_finite_type applies and gives a long exact sequence
\[\cdots\to H^m(X_{k,\acute et},j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \ } H^m(X)\xrightarrow{i^*} H^m(Y)\xrightarrow{\ \ } H^{m+1}(X_{k,\acute et},j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\cdots\qquad (\ast)_m\]
for every m\in\mathbb Z, in which the middle arrow is pullback along i. (For m<0 all groups H^m(X),H^m(Y) are 0, being right derived functors of \Gamma.)

STEP 2 (the term H^m(X_{k,\acute et},j_!\mathbb Q_\ell) is the usual compactly supported cohomology of U_k). Let p:U_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k and \pi:X_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k be the structure morphisms; \pi is proper because X is proper over \mathbb F_Q. We claim there is a canonical isomorphism in D(\operatorname{Spec}k)
\[Rp_!\mathbb Q_\ell\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;R\pi_*j_!\mathbb Q_\ell .\qquad(1)\]
Indeed p=\pi\circ j with j an open immersion and both morphisms separated of finite type, so the standard composition isomorphism for cohomology with proper supports gives Rp_!\cong R\pi_!\circ Rj_!; for an open immersion j the functor j_! on sheaves is exact and Rj_!=j_!, and for a proper morphism \pi the functor R\pi_! coincides canonically with R\pi_* (proper supports are automatic for a universally closed map). Thus Rp_!\mathbb Q_\ell\cong R\pi_*j_!\mathbb Q_\ell, and taking hypercohomology over \operatorname{Spec}k gives canonical isomorphisms
\[H^m_{\acute et,c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell):=H^m(\operatorname{Spec}k,Rp_!\mathbb Q_\ell)\;\cong\;H^m(X_{k,\acute et},j_!\mathbb Q_\ell),\]
which we use to rewrite (\ast)_m as
\[\cdots\to H^m_c(U)\to H^m(X)\xrightarrow{i^*} H^m(Y)\to H^{m+1}_c(U)\to\cdots .\qquad(2)_m\]
Both sides of (1) are functorial for morphisms over \mathbb F_Q (the construction uses only j_!, R\pi_* and the composition isomorphism, all natural), so (2) is compatible with Frobenius pullback, as made explicit in Step 4.

STEP 3 (computation of H^*_c(U) as a Frobenius module). By hypothesis U is isomorphic over \mathbb F_Q to a finite disjoint union \bigsqcup_{\beta\in B}\mathbb A^{e_\beta}_{\mathbb F_Q}. Each \mathbb A^{e_\beta} is connected, so the images of the factors are exactly the connected components of U, each defined over \mathbb F_Q and \mathbb F_Q-isomorphic to an affine space; by definition n_r=\#\{\beta\in B:e_\beta=r\}. Base change to k preserves the disjoint-union decomposition and each \mathbb A^{e_\beta}_k is connected, so the components of U_k are the C_\beta:=\mathbb A^{e_\beta}_k, and the same formula n_r=\#\{\beta:e_\beta=r\} counts them by dimension.

(a) Additivity. Applying Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum to the open-and-closed subscheme C_{\beta_1}\subseteq U_k with complement the union of the remaining (finitely many) components, and iterating on the number of components, gives for every m a canonical isomorphism (a finite direct sum of restriction maps)
\[H^m_c(U)\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;\bigoplus_{\beta\in B}H^m_c(\mathbb A^{e_\beta}_k).\qquad(3)\]
By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_hc_affine_space, H^m_c(\mathbb A^{s}_k)=0 for m\neq 2s and \dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^{2s}_c(\mathbb A^{s}_k)=1. Hence
\[H^{2r}_c(U)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell^{\,n_r},\qquad H^{2r+1}_c(U)=0\quad\text{for all }r\ge 0.\qquad(4)\]
(If U=\varnothing, i.e. B=\varnothing, the empty direct sum is 0 and (4) reads H^m_c(U)=0 for all m, which is correct since j_!\mathbb Q_\ell=0.)

(b) Frobenius eigenvalues. The isomorphism (3) is Frobenius-equivariant: it is built from restriction maps along open-and-closed immersions which are base changes of morphisms over \mathbb F_Q, and for any \mathbb F_Q-morphism g:Z\to Z' one has (\mathrm{id}\times\sigma)\circ g_k=g_k\circ(\mathrm{id}\times\sigma), so g_k^* intertwines F_{Z'} and F_Z (this is the functoriality behind eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a, which also says these pullbacks are \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphisms). Each summand H^{2s}_c(\mathbb A^{s}_k) is stable under F, and by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_286 the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius acts on it as multiplication by the scalar Q^{s}. Consequently F acts on H^{2r}_c(U) as Q^{r}\cdot\mathrm{id}, and on H^{2r+1}_c(U)=0 trivially. Therefore the characteristic polynomial of F on H^{2r}_c(U) is
\[\chi\bigl(F\mid H^{2r}_c(U)\bigr)(T)=(T-Q^{r})^{n_r}.\qquad(5)\]

STEP 4 (Frobenius-equivariance of the sequence (2)). The triple (X_k,Y_k,U_k) is defined over \mathbb F_Q, so f:=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma) is a morphism of pairs f_X:X_k\to X_k, f_Y:Y_k\to Y_k, f_U:U_k\to U_k with f_X\circ i=i\circ f_Y and f_X\circ j=j\circ f_U. The long exact sequence (2) is natural for morphisms of such triples (it is induced by the distinguished triangle Rj_!\mathbb Q_\ell\to\mathbb Q_\ell\to Ri_*\mathbb Q_\ell\to, whose construction is functorial, together with (1)), hence every arrow in (2) commutes with the operators F_{U},F_{X},F_{Y}. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a these operators are \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphisms of the respective groups, so the subspaces occurring as images/kernels below are F-stable.

STEP 5 (the short exact sequence in degree 2r). Fix r\ge 0. In (2)_{2r} we have H^{2r-1}(Y)=0: for r\ge 1 this is the hypothesis with 2(r-1)+1=2r-1, and for r=0 it is the vanishing of negative \acute etale cohomology. Also H^{2r+1}_c(U)=0 by (4). Exactness of
\[H^{2r-1}(Y)=0\to H^{2r}_c(U)\to H^{2r}(X)\xrightarrow{i^*}H^{2r}(Y)\to H^{2r+1}_c(U)=0\]
gives a short exact sequence
\[0\to H^{2r}_c(U)\longrightarrow H^{2r}(X)\xrightarrow{i^*} H^{2r}(Y)\to 0,\qquad(6)\]
and by Step 4 all three maps are Frobenius-equivariant, so W:=\operatorname{im}H^{2r}_c(U)\cong H^{2r}_c(U) is an F-stable subspace of V:=H^{2r}(X) with V/W\cong H^{2r}(Y) as F-modules. By hypothesis V and H^{2r}(Y) are finite-dimensional; W is 1-dimensional per summand by (4), so all terms are finite-dimensional.

STEP 6 (multiplicativity of the characteristic polynomial in a short exact sequence). We record the elementary fact used to conclude, and prove it. Let K be a field, 0\to W\to V\to Q\to 0 a short exact sequence of finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, and T\in\operatorname{End}_K(V) with T(W)\subseteq W; let \bar T be the induced endomorphism of Q. Then \chi_{T,V}(t)=\chi_{T|_W}(t)\,\chi_{\bar T}(t) in K[t]. Proof: choose a basis w_1,\dots,w_a of W and vectors v_1,\dots,v_b\in V whose classes \bar v_1,\dots,\bar v_b form a basis of Q; then w_1,\dots,w_a,v_1,\dots,v_b is a basis of V (the sequence is exact, so V is spanned and the dimensions add). Write T v_j=\sum_i \alpha_{ij}v_i+\sum_{i} \gamma_{ij}w_i and T w_j=\sum_i\beta_{ij}w_i (possible because W is T-stable). The matrix of T in this basis is block upper triangular, \(\begin{pmatrix}B&A\\0&C\end{pmatrix}\), where B=(\beta_{ij}) is the matrix of T|_W and C=(\alpha_{ij}) is the matrix of \bar T, because \bar T\bar v_j=\sum_i\alpha_{ij}\bar v_i. Hence tI-\begin{pmatrix}B&A\\0&C\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}tI-B&-A\\0&tI-C\end{pmatrix} has determinant \det(tI-B)\det(tI-C), which is the claimed product of characteristic polynomials. (No splitting or semisimplicity of T is needed.)

STEP 7 (conclusion). Apply Step 6 to K=\mathbb Q_\ell, V=H^{2r}(X), W=\operatorname{im}H^{2r}_c(U) and T=F_X. The characteristic polynomial of T|_W equals that of F on H^{2r}_c(U), namely (T_0-Q^{r})^{n_r} by (5) (here T_0 is the indeterminate; we write the polynomial variable as T_0 to avoid confusion with the operator, and identify W with H^{2r}_c(U) via the injective localisation map). The characteristic polynomial of \bar T on V/W\cong H^{2r}(Y) is P_r(T_0), by the hypothesis on Y together with the Frobenius-equivariance of the isomorphism V/W\xrightarrow{\sim}H^{2r}(Y) from (6). Since \mathbb Q_\ell[T_0] is commutative,
\[\chi\bigl(F_X\mid H^{2r}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)(T_0)=P_r(T_0)\,(T_0-Q^{r})^{n_r},\]
which is exactly the required statement, for every r\ge 0. \(
\)
All edge cases are covered: r=0 (where H^{-1}(Y)=0 and H^0_c(U) is \mathbb Q_\ell^{n_0} with F acting as Q^0=1, so the factor is (T_0-1)^{n_0}); n_r=0 (the factor is 1 and (6) is an isomorphism); U=\varnothing (H^*_c(U)=0 and (6) identifies H^{2r}(X) with H^{2r}(Y)); and negative degrees, which contribute only zero groups.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(x\in X\) be a closed point, and let \(\pi:X'=\operatorname{Bl}_x X\to X\) be the blow-up. Let \(F_X\) and \(F_{X'}\) be the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms \((\operatorname{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), on \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(F_X\) is semisimple on \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) if and only if \(F_{X'}\) is semisimple on \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
proof:
Write $\mathbb F:=\mathbb F_{q^m}$ for the ground field, $K:=\kappa(x)$ for the residue field of the closed point $x$, and $r:=[K:\mathbb F]\ge 1$. Let $\Phi_Z:=(\operatorname{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ with $\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}$ denote the $\mathbb F$-rational ($=q^m$-power) arithmetic Frobenius on the étale cohomology of $Z_k$; thus $\Phi_Z=F_Z$ for $Z\in\{X,X'\}$, and we also write $\Phi_x$ for the same operator on $H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(x_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

**Step 1: the blow-up formula in degree 2.**
We claim the hypotheses of eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/3a81bf are satisfied with $d=2$ and $B=x$. Indeed:
- $q=p^a$ is a prime power, $\ell\neq p$, $m\ge 1$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, and $d=2\ge 2$;
- $X$ is smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension $2$ over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, by hypothesis;
- $B=x=\operatorname{Spec}K$ is a closed subscheme of $X$ via the canonical (reduced, closed) immersion. Since $x$ is a closed point of a scheme of finite type over the field $\mathbb F$, Zariski's lemma gives that $K/\mathbb F$ is finite; $\mathbb F$ is perfect, so $K/\mathbb F$ is finite separable, hence $\operatorname{Spec}K\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F$ is finite étale, in particular smooth. Thus $x$ is a nonempty smooth closed subvariety, defined over $\mathbb F=\mathbb F_{q^m}$, of pure dimension $0=d-2$;
- $\pi:X'=\operatorname{Bl}_x X\to X$ is exactly the blow-up of $X$ along $B$ required by that lemma.

Applying eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/3a81bf with these data yields the equivalence
$$
\Phi_{X'}\text{ is semisimple on }H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)
\iff
\bigl[\ \Phi_X\text{ is semisimple on }H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\ \text{ and }\ \Phi_x\text{ is semisimple on }H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(x_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\ \bigr].
\eqno{(1)}
$$
So the whole claim reduces to the following unconditional fact.

**Step 2: $\Phi_x$ is semisimple on $H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(x_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.**

*2a. The geometric fibre of $x$.* Choose a monic irreducible polynomial $f\in\mathbb F[T]$ of degree $r$ with $K\simeq\mathbb F[T]/(f)$. Then
$$A:=K\otimes_{\mathbb F}k\ \simeq\ k[T]/(f).$$
Since $k$ is algebraically closed and $f$ is separable (characteristic $p$ field $\mathbb F$ is perfect), $f$ factors in $k[T]$ as $f(T)=\prod_{j=0}^{r-1}(T-\alpha_j)$ with $r$ pairwise distinct roots. They form one Frobenius orbit: fixing a root $\alpha_0$, the set of roots is $\{\alpha_j:=\alpha_0^{\,q^{mj}}:0\le j\le r-1\}$, because the map $j\mapsto\alpha_j$ gives $r$ distinct roots of $f$ (an irreducible polynomial over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ has its roots exactly in the $q^m$-Frobenius orbit of any one of them, of length $r$). By the Chinese remainder theorem,
$$A\ \simeq\ \prod_{j=0}^{r-1}k[T]/(T-\alpha_j)\ \simeq\ k^{\,r},$$\nso $x_k=\operatorname{Spec}A=\coprod_{j=0}^{r-1}\operatorname{Spec}k$ is a disjoint union of $r$ copies of $\operatorname{Spec}k$; its maximal ideals (equivalently its connected components) are $\mathfrak m_j=(T-\alpha_j)$, $j\in\mathbb Z/r\mathbb Z$.

*2b. The permutation of components.* The morphism $\Phi_x=\operatorname{id}_x\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$ corresponds to the ring automorphism $\varphi:=\operatorname{id}_K\otimes\sigma$ of $A$. Under the above identification $A\simeq k[T]/(f)$,
$$\varphi\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_i c_i T^i\Bigr)=\textstyle\sum_i c_i^{\,q^m}T^i,$$\nsince $\varphi(T^i\otimes c_i)=T^i\otimes c_i^{q^m}$. This is well defined because $f$ has coefficients in $\mathbb F=\mathbb F_{q^m}$, so $f^\sigma=f$. For $g=\sum_i c_iT^i\in A$ we compute, writing $\beta_j:=\alpha_j^{\,q^{-m}}\in k$ (the unique $q^m$-th root of $\alpha_j$ in $k$):
$$g^\sigma\in\mathfrak m_j\iff g^\sigma(\alpha_j)=0\iff \textstyle\sum_i c_i^{q^m}\alpha_j^{\,i}=0\iff\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_i c_i\beta_j^{\,i}\Bigr)^{q^m}=0\iff g(\beta_j)=0\iff g\in (T-\beta_j).$$
Hence $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak m_j)=(T-\alpha_j^{q^{-m}})$. As $\alpha_j=\alpha_0^{q^{mj}}$, we have $\alpha_j^{q^{-m}}=\alpha_0^{q^{m(j-1)}}=\alpha_{j-1}$, so
$$\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak m_j)=\mathfrak m_{j-1}\qquad(\text{indices in }\mathbb Z/r\mathbb Z).\eqno{(2)}$$
Thus the homeomorphism $\Phi_x$ of the underlying space of $x_k$ acts on $\pi_0(x_k)=\{\mathfrak m_0,\dots,\mathfrak m_{r-1}\}$ as the cyclic permutation $\mathfrak m_j\mapsto\mathfrak m_{j+1}$, which has order dividing $r$. Consequently $\Phi_x^{\,r}$ fixes every connected component of $x_k$ (and restricts on each component to a morphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$).

*2c. The induced action on $H^0$.* Because $k$ is separably closed, $H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\operatorname{Spec}k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell$ (global sections of the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ are the locally constant functions on $\pi_0(\operatorname{Spec}k)=\{*\}$), and for a morphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ the pullback on $H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(-,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is the identity of $\mathbb Q_\ell$, since inverse image of a constant sheaf along any morphism is the constant sheaf and the induced map on sections is the identity on the coefficient group. As $x_k$ is the disjoint union of the $r$ components, global sections add:
$$H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(x_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\ \simeq\ \bigoplus_{j=0}^{r-1}\mathbb Q_\ell\,e_j,$$\nwhere $e_j$ is the characteristic function of the component $\operatorname{Spec}k$ indexed by $\mathfrak m_j$. Pullback along $\Phi_x$ acts by precomposition with the map on components, i.e. by (2), $\Phi_x^*(e_j)=e_{j-1}$. Hence $\Phi_x^*$ is the matrix of a permutation of the basis $\{e_j\}$ of order dividing $r$, and therefore
$$\bigl(\Phi_x^*\bigr)^{r}=\operatorname{id}\ \ \text{on}\ \ H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(x_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).\eqno{(3)}$$
(In particular $\Phi_x^*$ is invertible, as it must be for an automorphism.)

*2d. Semisimplicity.* The $r$-th power $\bigl(\Phi_x^*\bigr)^r$ is the identity by (3); the base change of the identity to $H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(x_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is diagonalisable. Apply Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/54a945 with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ (a field of characteristic $0$), $V=H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(x_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (finite dimensional, of dimension $r$), $T=\Phi_x^*\in\operatorname{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$ and $s=r$: since the base change of $T^r$ to $V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is diagonalisable, so is the base change of $T$. Finally, by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5, an operator on a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space is semisimple if and only if its base change to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is diagonalisable. Thus
$$\Phi_x\ \text{is semisimple on }H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(x_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).\eqno{(4)}$$

**Step 3: conclusion.** Insert (4) into the equivalence (1). The right-hand side of (1) is a conjunction $P\wedge Q$ with $Q$ true, hence equivalent to $P$. Therefore
$$\Phi_{X'}\text{ is semisimple on }H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\iff \Phi_X\text{ is semisimple on }H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),$$\nwhich, in the notation of the statement ($F_X=\Phi_X$, $F_{X'}=\Phi_{X'}$), is exactly the required equivalence. Both directions are covered: semisimplicity of $F_X$ implies that of $F_{X'}$ by $(1)$ together with (4), and conversely semisimplicity of $F_{X'}$ implies that of $F_X$ by the forward implication of $(1)$. $\blacksquare$

*Remark on the argument's scope.* Only degree $2$ on $X$ and $X'$, and degree $0$ on the centre, are used; no statement about other degrees, no weak factorisation, and no rationality of $x$ is needed. The point $x$ is allowed to have arbitrary residue degree $r$, and the whole contribution of the non-rational centre is the extra summand $H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(x_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, on which Frobenius acts as a permutation matrix of finite order, hence semisimply.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let l != p be prime, let m>=1, and put k=overline(F_q). Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over F_{q^m}, let Z be a smooth closed subvariety of X of pure codimension c>=1 defined over F_{q^m}, and let pi:Bl_Z X -> X be the blow-up. If the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et((Bl_Z X)_k,Q_l) for every integer n>=0, then it is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) for every integer n>=0.
proof:
Let Q = q^m and Y = Bl_Z X. Then Q is a prime power and k is the algebraic closure of F_Q. The Frobenius in the statement is the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius. If Z is empty, pi is the identity and the conclusion is immediate. Assume Z is nonempty.

We first check that pi:Y -> X satisfies the hypotheses of the birational pullback lemma. Since X is smooth projective over F_Q and Z is a smooth closed subscheme of pure codimension c >= 1, Y is smooth and projective over F_Q: blow-up of a smooth variety along a smooth center is smooth (étale-locally one blows up affine space along a linear subspace, whose charts are affine spaces), and blow-up of a projective scheme along a closed subscheme is projective. The morphism pi is defined over F_Q because Z is. It is birational because it is an isomorphism over the open subset X - Z, and this open subset is dense: X is smooth and geometrically connected, hence geometrically integral (smoothness gives regular local rings and therefore local irreducibility; connectedness of X_k gives irreducibility, and smoothness gives reducedness), while Z is a proper closed subset. Moreover Y is geometrically connected. Indeed, blow-up commutes with flat base change, so Y_k is the blow-up of X_k along Z_k. The scheme X_k is integral. The blow-up of an integral scheme is integral, so pi_k:Y_k -> X_k is proper birational. Since X_k is smooth, it is normal; for a proper birational morphism to a normal scheme one has pi_k*O_{Y_k} = O_{X_k}. Therefore H^0(Y_k,O) = H^0(X_k,O) = k, where the last equality uses that X_k is connected and proper over the algebraically closed field k. Since Y_k is smooth and proper over k, its ring of global functions is reduced; the equality H^0(Y_k,O)=k implies that Y_k has no nontrivial idempotents, hence Y_k is connected. Thus Y is smooth projective geometrically connected and has the same pure dimension as X.

All cohomology groups below are finite-dimensional Q_ℓ-vector spaces by finiteness of étale cohomology of proper varieties. For each n >= 0, write V_n = H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ℓ), W_n = H^n_et(X_k,Q_ℓ), T_n = F_Y on V_n, and S_n = F_X on W_n, where F_Y and F_X are the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms (id × Spec σ)^*, σ(t)=t^Q. By the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_414, applied with q replaced by Q to the F_Q-birational morphism pi:Y -> X, the pullback pi^*:W_n -> V_n is injective and there exists a Q_ℓ-linear map s_n:V_n -> W_n such that s_n o pi^* = id and s_n o T_n = S_n o s_n.

Because pi is defined over F_Q, pullback commutes with arithmetic Frobenius: pi^* o S_n = T_n o pi^*. Hence U_n = pi^*(W_n) is a T_n-stable subspace of V_n, and pi^*:W_n -> U_n is an isomorphism of vector spaces satisfying pi^*(S_n w) = T_n(pi^* w) for all w in W_n.

Let p_n = pi^* o s_n:V_n -> V_n. Then p_n is a projection onto U_n: p_n^2 = p_n and im(p_n) = U_n. It is T_n-equivariant, since p_n o T_n = pi^* o s_n o T_n = pi^* o S_n o s_n = T_n o pi^* o s_n = T_n o p_n. Therefore V_n = U_n ⊕ ker(p_n) as T_n-modules, so U_n is a T_n-stable direct summand of V_n.

By hypothesis T_n is semisimple on V_n for every n. By the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_35, part (ii), the restriction T_n|_{U_n} is semisimple on U_n. Under the T_n-equivariant isomorphism pi^*:W_n -> U_n, this restriction corresponds exactly to S_n. Therefore S_n is semisimple on W_n. Since n was arbitrary, the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ℓ) for every n >= 0, which is precisely the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(Y\subset X\) be a smooth effective divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), geometrically connected and of pure dimension \(d-1\), with closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\). For \(0\le m\le 2d-2\) let \(f_m:H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{m+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the Gysin homomorphism for \(i\), characterised by \(\operatorname{tr}_X(f_m a\cup b)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(a\cup i^*b)\) for every \(b\in H^{2d-2-m}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), where \(\operatorname{tr}_Z\) is the Poincar\'e duality trace normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\). Fix a nonzero \(u\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and let \(T_u:H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-1)\to H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) send \(a\otimes u^{-1}\) to \(a\). Then \(f_m\circ T_u\) commutes with the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius, where Frobenius on \(H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-1)\) is \(F_Y\otimes F_{\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)}\) with \(F_{\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)}\) the multiplication by \(q\).
proof:
We write \(H^n(Z):=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\), \(D_X:=\dim X=d\) and \(D_Y:=\dim Y=d-1\), and we denote by \(F_X=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\) and \(F_Y=(\mathrm{id}_{Y_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius operators on \(H^*(X)\) and \(H^*(Y)\). Both are automorphisms of the graded \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-algebras by lemma_6a. The statement's traces are \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-valued \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear functionals \(\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2D_Z}(Z)\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) (the adjunction in the statement is an identity of elements of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\), as is the normalisation \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\in\mathbb Q_\ell\)).

STEP 1 (Tate-twist bookkeeping; reduction to a relation for \(f_m\)).
Since \(u\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) is nonzero and \(\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(1)=1\), the element \(u^{-1}:=(u\mapsto 1)\in\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(\mathbb Q_\ell(1),\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-basis of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)\). Hence \(T_u:H^m(Y)(-1)=H^m(Y)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^m(Y)\), \(a\otimes u^{-1}\mapsto a\), is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism (inverse \(a\mapsto a\otimes u^{-1}\)); in particular it is surjective.
Let \(\Phi:=F_Y\otimes F_{\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)}\) be the Frobenius on \(H^m(Y)(-1)\) specified in the statement, so \(F_{\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)}(u^{-1})=q\,u^{-1}\). For a pure tensor \(a\otimes u^{-1}\) we compute
\[
\Phi(a\otimes u^{-1})=F_Ya\otimes q\,u^{-1}=q\,(F_Ya\otimes u^{-1}),
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
T_u\Phi(a\otimes u^{-1})=q\,F_Ya=q\,F_YT_u(a\otimes u^{-1}).
\]
Since such tensors generate \(H^m(Y)(-1)\), this is an identity of operators:
\[
\tag{1} T_u\circ\Phi=q\,F_Y\circ T_u .
\]
Put \(G_u:=f_m\circ T_u:H^m(Y)(-1)\to H^{m+2}(X)\). The required conclusion \(G_u\circ\Phi=F_X\circ G_u\) is, by (1),
\[
f_m\circ T_u\circ\Phi=F_X\circ f_m\circ T_u\iff q\,f_m\circ F_Y\circ T_u=F_X\circ f_m\circ T_u .
\]
As \(T_u\) is surjective, the right-hand equivalence is with \(q\,f_m\circ F_Y=F_X\circ f_m\), i.e.
\[
\tag{\dagger} f_m\circ F_Y=q^{-1}\,F_X\circ f_m .
\]
Thus it suffices to prove \((\dagger)\).

STEP 2 (two formal consequences of the statement's traces; no convention comparison).
Fix \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\). Both \(X\) and \(Y\) are smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension over \(\mathbb F_q\) (for \(Y\) this uses the hypothesis that \(Y\) is geometrically connected; when \(d=1\), \(Y\) is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension \(0\), which is still within the scope of the lemmas quoted below).

(2a) *Perfection.* By lemma_77(a) applied with \(m=1\) (over \(\mathbb F_{q^1}=\mathbb F_q\)) to \(Z\), the canonical trace \(\tau_Z:H^{2D_Z}(Z)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell(-D_Z)\) is an isomorphism; hence \(\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^{2D_Z}(Z)=1\). Choose any \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector-space isomorphism \(\psi_Z:\mathbb Q_\ell(-D_Z)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell\). The functional \(\operatorname{tr}_Z\) is nonzero, because for any closed point \(z\in Z\) (such exist, and \(Z\neq\varnothing\) since \(Y\) is an effective divisor and \(X\) has positive dimension) the normalisation gives \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\ge 1\), a positive integer, hence nonzero in \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Being two nonzero \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear functionals on a \(1\)-dimensional space, there is a scalar \(\lambda_Z\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\) with
\[
\operatorname{tr}_Z=\lambda_Z\cdot\psi_Z\circ\tau_Z .
\]
By lemma_77(b) (again with \(m=1\)) the \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-D_Z)\)-valued pairing \((x,y)\mapsto\tau_Z(x\cup y)\) on \(H^n(Z)\times H^{2D_Z-n}(Z)\) is perfect for every \(0\le n\le 2D_Z\); i.e. the induced map \(H^n(Z)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^{2D_Z-n}(Z),\mathbb Q_\ell(-D_Z))\) is an isomorphism. Composing this target with the isomorphism \((\psi_Z)_*\) induced by \(\psi_Z\) shows that \((x,y)\mapsto\psi_Z\tau_Z(x\cup y)\) is a perfect \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-valued pairing, and multiplying a perfect pairing by the nonzero scalar \(\lambda_Z\) preserves perfection. Therefore
\[
\tag{2} \langle x,y\rangle_Z:=\operatorname{tr}_Z(x\cup y)\ \text{is a perfect pairing } H^n(Z)\times H^{2D_Z-n}(Z)\to\mathbb Q_\ell\ \text{for every }0\le n\le 2D_Z .
\]
In particular, if \(x\in H^n(Z)\) satisfies \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(x\cup w)=0\) for every \(w\in H^{2D_Z-n}(Z)\), then \(x=0\).

(2b) *Frobenius on the top degree.* By lemma_199 applied to \(Z\) (\(D=D_Z\)), \(F_Z\) acts on \(H^{2D_Z}(Z)\) as multiplication by \(q^{D_Z}\). Since \(\operatorname{tr}_Z\) is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear,
\[
\tag{3} \operatorname{tr}_Z(F_Z\gamma)=q^{D_Z}\operatorname{tr}_Z(\gamma)\qquad\text{for every }\gamma\in H^{2D_Z}(Z) .
\]
Note that no assertion is made here about how \(\operatorname{tr}_Z\) behaves on products of arbitrary degrees; only (3) is used.

STEP 3 (formal compatibilities of Frobenius with cup product and with \(i\)).
(a) \(F_Z\) is pullback along the morphism of schemes \(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma:Z_k\to Z_k\); functoriality of the cup product under pullback gives \(F_Z(\alpha\cup\beta)=F_Z\alpha\cup F_Z\beta\) for all \(\alpha,\beta\in H^*(Z)\).
(b) The divisor \(Y\) and the immersion \(i\) are defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), so \(i_k:Y_k\to X_k\) satisfies \(i_k\circ(\mathrm{id}_{Y_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)\circ i_k\) (equality of the two composites \(Y_k=Y\times_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k\to X_k\), both being \(i\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma\)). Taking contravariant pullbacks,
\[
\tag{4} i^*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ i^*\ \ \text{on } H^*(X).
\]

STEP 4 (proof of \((\dagger)\)).
Fix \(m\) with \(0\le m\le 2d-2\), fix \(a\in H^m(Y)\), and let \(b\in H^{2d-2-m}(X)\) be arbitrary; put \(c:=F_Xb\). By lemma_6a, \(F_X\) is an automorphism of \(H^{2d-2-m}(X)\), so \(c\) runs over all of \(H^{2d-2-m}(X)\) as \(b\) does.
Degree checks: \(a\cup i^*b\in H^{m+(2d-2-m)}(Y)=H^{2d-2}(Y)=H^{2D_Y}(Y)\); \(f_ma\cup b\in H^{(m+2)+(2d-2-m)}(X)=H^{2d}(X)=H^{2D_X}(X)\). Hence (3) applies to both.

First computation, using (4), then 3(a), then (3) for \(Y\) with \(D_Y=d-1\), then the adjunction defining \(f_m\) (valid for every \(b\in H^{2d-2-m}(X)\)):
\[
\operatorname{tr}_Y(F_Ya\cup i^*c)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(F_Ya\cup F_Yi^*b)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(F_Y(a\cup i^*b)\bigr)=q^{d-1}\operatorname{tr}_Y(a\cup i^*b)=q^{d-1}\operatorname{tr}_X(f_ma\cup b).
\]
Second computation, using 3(a) and then (3) for \(X\) with \(D_X=d\):
\[
\operatorname{tr}_X(F_Xf_ma\cup c)=\operatorname{tr}_X(F_Xf_ma\cup F_Xb)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(F_X(f_ma\cup b)\bigr)=q^{d}\operatorname{tr}_X(f_ma\cup b).
\]
Eliminating \(\operatorname{tr}_X(f_ma\cup b)\) between the two displayed lines gives \(\operatorname{tr}_X(F_Xf_ma\cup c)=q\cdot q^{d-1}\operatorname{tr}_X(f_ma\cup b)=q\,\operatorname{tr}_Y(F_Ya\cup i^*c)\). Applying the adjunction defining \(f_m\) to the class \(F_Ya\in H^m(Y)\) and the element \(c\in H^{2d-2-m}(X)\) turns the last term into \(q\,\operatorname{tr}_X(f_mF_Ya\cup c)\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl((F_Xf_ma-q\,f_mF_Ya)\cup c\bigr)=0\qquad\text{for every }c\in H^{2d-2-m}(X).
\]
The class \(F_Xf_ma-q\,f_mF_Ya\) lies in \(H^{m+2}(X)\), and \((m+2)+(2d-2-m)=2d=2D_X\) with \(0\le m+2\le 2d\); by the perfection (2) of the \(X\)-pairing in degrees \((m+2,\,2d-2-m)\) we conclude
\[
F_Xf_ma=q\,f_mF_Ya\qquad\text{for every }a\in H^m(Y),
\]
i.e. \(f_m\circ F_Y=q^{-1}F_X\circ f_m\), which is \((\dagger)\).

Edge case \(d=1\): then necessarily \(m=0\), \(D_Y=0\), and the same argument runs verbatim: lemma_199 with \(D=0\) says \(F_Y\) acts on \(H^0(Y)\) as \(q^0=1\), and (2) with \(n=2\) for \(X\) gives the needed non-degeneracy \(H^2(X)\times H^0(X)\to\mathbb Q_\ell\). No separate treatment is required.

STEP 5 (conclusion).
Substituting \((\dagger)\) into the equivalence established in Step 1 yields, for every \(\xi\in H^m(Y)(-1)\),
\[
G_u\Phi(\xi)=f_MT_u\Phi(\xi)=q\,f_mF_YT_u(\xi)=F_Xf_MT_u(\xi)=F_XG_u(\xi),
\]
so \(f_m\circ T_u\) commutes with the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius (acting as \(F_Y\otimes F_{\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)}\) on \(H^m(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-1)\) and as \(F_X\) on \(H^{m+2}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\)). This is exactly the claim.

(Remark on what was *not* used: the proof never identifies \(f_m\) with any other Gysin map, never compares \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-D_Z)\)-valued with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-valued traces beyond the scalar-multiple observation in (2a), and never uses the normalisation of \(\operatorname{tr}_Y\) on geometric components; the only properties of the given traces used are perfection (2) and the top-degree scaling (3).)

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(Y\subset X\) be a nonempty effective smooth ample divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) that is geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\), and let \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) be the closed immersion. Then \(i^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every integer \(n<d-1\) and is injective for \(n=d-1\).
proof:
Proof. Set Q = q^m = p^{am}. Then Q is again a prime power, X and Y are defined over F_Q, and the algebraic closure of F_Q is the same field k = overline(F_Q). Let U = X - Y be the open complement of Y in X.

First apply the proved lemma eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/9185a1. Its hypotheses are satisfied: X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d >= 2 over F_{q^m}, Y is a nonempty smooth ample divisor defined over F_{q^m}, and U is its complement. Therefore, for every integer j < d, one has H_c^j(U_k, Q_l) = 0.

Next apply the proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_283 with the prime power Q in place of its q. This is legitimate because Q is a prime power and its algebraic closure is k. The lemma gives, for every integer n >= 0, an exact sequence
H_c^n(U_k, Q_l) -> H^n(X_k, Q_l) --i^*--> H^n(Y_k, Q_l) -> H_c^{n+1}(U_k, Q_l),
where the middle arrow is pullback along the closed immersion i: Y -> X. For n < 0, etale cohomology groups are zero by definition, so the desired assertions are automatic in negative degrees.

Now take any integer n < d-1. If n < 0, then both H^n(X_k, Q_l) and H^n(Y_k, Q_l) are zero, so i^* is an isomorphism. Assume n >= 0. Since n < d-1, we have n <= d-2, hence n < d and n+1 < d. By the vanishing above, H_c^n(U_k, Q_l) = 0 and H_c^{n+1}(U_k, Q_l) = 0. The exact sequence therefore becomes
0 -> H^n(X_k, Q_l) --i^*--> H^n(Y_k, Q_l) -> 0.
Thus i^* is an isomorphism for every n < d-1.

Finally take n = d-1. Since d-1 < d, the vanishing above gives H_c^{d-1}(U_k, Q_l) = 0. The exact sequence begins
0 -> H^{d-1}(X_k, Q_l) --i^*--> H^{d-1}(Y_k, Q_l).
Exactness at H^{d-1}(X_k, Q_l) says that the kernel of i^* is the image of the preceding zero map, hence the kernel is zero. Therefore i^* is injective for n = d-1.

This proves that i^*: H^n_et(X_k, Q_l) -> H^n_et(Y_k, Q_l) is an isomorphism for every integer n < d-1 and is injective for n = d-1. QED.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_q\). Then the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{S_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), is semisimple on \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
proof:
Let k = bar(F_q). Since S is projective over F_q, choose an ample line bundle L on S defined over F_q. Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_437 to X = S, d = 2, and L. It gives integers m >= 1, r >= 1 and a section s in H^0(S_{F_{q^m}}, L^{otimes r}) whose zero scheme Y = V(s) is a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor on S_{F_{q^m}}, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension 1 over F_{q^m}. Being a closed subscheme of the projective variety S_{F_{q^m}}, Y is projective; hence Y is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_{q^m}. Put X_m = S_{F_{q^m}} and let i:Y -> X_m be the closed immersion. The base change X_m is smooth and projective of pure dimension 2 over F_{q^m}; it is geometrically connected because after further base change to k it is S_k, which is connected.

By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob, applied to the proper varieties S, X_m, and Y (with q replaced by q^m where appropriate), the groups H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell), H^1_et((X_m)_k,Q_ell), and H^1_et(Y_k,Q_ell) are finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector spaces, and the corresponding arithmetic Frobenius maps are invertible Q_ell-linear automorphisms. We identify (X_m)_k with S_k via the canonical base-change isomorphism S_{F_{q^m}} times_{F_{q^m}} k = S times_{F_q} k.

Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_364 to the curve Y with n = 1. The q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F_Y on H^1_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is semisimple.

Apply eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/f527bc to X_m, the divisor Y, and d = 2. For n = d - 1 = 1, its conclusion says that the restriction map i^*: H^1_et((X_m)_k,Q_ell) -> H^1_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is injective and is equivariant for the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. Let F_m denote the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell) under the above identification. Equivariance means i^* F_m = F_Y i^*. Set W = i^*(H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell)) subset H^1_et(Y_k,Q_ell). If w = i^*x in W, then F_Y w = i^*(F_m x) in W, so W is F_Y-stable.

By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_515, the restriction F_Y|_W is semisimple. The map i^*: H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell) -> W is a Q_ell-linear isomorphism and intertwines F_m with F_Y|_W. Hence by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8, F_m is semisimple on H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell).

It remains to pass from the q^m-power Frobenius to the q-power Frobenius. Let sigma:k -> k be sigma(c) = c^q, let f = (id_{S_k} times Spec sigma), and let F = (id_{S_k} times Spec sigma)^* = f^* be the q-power arithmetic Frobenius. Since sigma^m(c) = c^{q^m}, the morphism defining F_m is f^m = (id_{S_k} times Spec sigma^m). Functoriality of etale cohomology pullbacks gives (f^m)^* = (f^*)^m, because (g o h)^* = h^* o g^* and an induction on m yields the equality. Thus F_m = F^m.

We have shown that F^m is semisimple on the finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell), and F is invertible by the Frobenius automorphism statement above. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_35, part (iii), if an invertible operator has a semisimple positive power, then the operator itself is semisimple. Therefore F is semisimple on H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell). This is exactly the desired conclusion.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\subset \mathbb P^{d+1}_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\) be a smooth geometrically connected hypersurface of pure dimension \(d\ge1\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and use it to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of \(\mathcal O_X(1)\), and let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\). Then \(L^{d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every integer \(n\) with \(0\le n\le d\).
proof:
We prove the statement by verifying that a smooth geometrically connected hypersurface X \subset \mathbb P^{d+1}_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} admits a smooth flag of length one, namely X = Y_1 \subset Y_0 = \mathbb P^{d+1}_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}, and then applying Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_hard_lefschetz_from_smooth_flag with c = 1.

Step 0 (notation and parameters). Put F = \mathbb F_{q^m}, k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q, and take c = 1, so that d + c = d + 1 and d \ge 1 by hypothesis. The candidate chain of closed subschemes is
   Y_1 := X \ \subset\ Y_0 := \mathbb P^{d+1}_{F}.

Step 1 (the top member Y_0 is smooth, geometrically connected, of pure dimension d+1). Projective space \mathbb P^{d+1}_{F} is smooth over F (it is covered by affine spaces \mathbb A^{d+1}_F), it is geometrically integral over F (for every field extension F'/F the homogeneous coordinate ring F'[T_0,\dots,T_{d+1}] is a domain, so \mathbb P^{d+1}_{F'} is integral), hence geometrically connected, and it is of pure dimension d+1 = d+c. Thus Y_0 satisfies the required properties.

Step 2 (the bottom member Y_1 = X is smooth, geometrically connected, of pure dimension d). This is exactly the hypothesis of the target lemma: X is a smooth geometrically connected hypersurface of pure dimension d \ge 1 over F = \mathbb F_{q^m}. In particular X is nonempty (a scheme of pure dimension d has an irreducible component of dimension d), and X \subsetneq \mathbb P^{d+1}_F is a proper closed subscheme (a nonempty proper closed subset of an irreducible space of dimension d+1 has dimension d).

Step 3 (X is an effective Cartier divisor on \mathbb P^{d+1}_F). Let I = I_X \subset \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{d+1}_F} be the ideal sheaf. We check that I is invertible and generated by a non-zero-divisor at every point of X.

First, X is integral: X is smooth over F, hence every local ring \mathcal O_{X,x} is regular, hence a domain; so X is locally integral. A locally integral noetherian scheme has pairwise disjoint irreducible components, each of which is open and closed; since X is connected (geometrically connected implies connected), X has a single irreducible component, i.e. X is integral.

Now fix x \in X and write A := \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{d+1}_F,x} and \mathfrak p := I_x \subsetneq A. Then:
 (a) A is a regular local ring (\mathbb P^{d+1}_F is smooth over F), hence a domain and a unique factorisation domain, and it is Cohen--Macaulay.
 (b) A/\mathfrak p = \mathcal O_{X,x} is a regular local ring, hence a domain, so \mathfrak p is a prime ideal.
 (c) ht(\mathfrak p) = 1. Indeed, in the Cohen--Macaulay (equidimensional, universally catenary) local ring A one has ht(\mathfrak p) = \dim A - \dim A/\mathfrak p. Since \mathbb P^{d+1}_F and X are integral schemes of finite type over F, the dimension formula for points of a variety gives \dim A = \dim \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{d+1}_F,x} = (d+1) - \operatorname{trdeg}_F \kappa(x) and \dim A/\mathfrak p = \dim \mathcal O_{X,x} = d - \operatorname{trdeg}_F \kappa(x). Hence ht(\mathfrak p) = (d+1 - \operatorname{trdeg}_F\kappa(x)) - (d - \operatorname{trdeg}_F\kappa(x)) = 1.

In a UFD every height-one prime ideal is principal, generated by an irreducible element; since A is a domain, that generator is a non-zero-divisor. Thus \mathfrak p = (f_x) with f_x a non-zero-divisor of A. As this holds at every x \in X (and I is the unit ideal off X), I is an invertible ideal sheaf and X is an effective Cartier divisor of \mathbb P^{d+1}_F.

Step 4 (the divisor is cut out by a section of O(e) with e \ge 1). The Picard group of projective space is Pic(\mathbb P^{d+1}_F) = \mathbb Z\cdot[\mathcal O(1)], so there is a unique integer e with I \simeq \mathcal O(-e).
 (i) e \ge 0: the inclusion I \hookrightarrow \mathcal O is a nonzero homomorphism \mathcal O(-e) \to \mathcal O, i.e. a nonzero element of H^0(\mathbb P^{d+1}_F, \mathcal O(e)); for e < 0 this space of global sections is 0, a contradiction.
 (ii) e \neq 0: if e = 0 then I \simeq \mathcal O and the inclusion is multiplication by a nonzero scalar in H^0(\mathcal O) = F^{\times}, hence an isomorphism I = \mathcal O, which would give X = \varnothing, contradicting Step 2.
 Hence e \ge 1.

Let s \in H^0(\mathbb P^{d+1}_F, \mathcal O(e)) = \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal O(-e), \mathcal O) be the section corresponding to the inclusion I \hookrightarrow \mathcal O. By definition the zero scheme Z(s) of s is the closed subscheme whose ideal sheaf is the image of \mathcal O(-e) \xrightarrow{\;s\;} \mathcal O, and that image is precisely I. Therefore Z(s) = X. Thus X = Y_1 is the zero scheme in Y_0 = \mathbb P^{d+1}_F of a section of \mathcal O_{Y_0}(e_1) with e_1 := e \ge 1.

Step 5 (apply the flag lemma). We have assembled exactly the hypotheses of Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_hard_lefschetz_from_smooth_flag with the integers c = 1 \ge 0 and d \ge 1, the prime power q, the prime \ell \neq p, the extension degree m, k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q, the smooth geometrically connected closed subscheme X \subset \mathbb P^{d+1}_F = \mathbb P^{d+c}_F of pure dimension d, the chain X = Y_1 \subset Y_0 = \mathbb P^{d+1}_F whose members are smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimensions d+1 and d over \mathbb F_{q^m}, the single integer e_1 = e \ge 1 with Y_1 the zero scheme in Y_0 of a section of \mathcal O_{Y_0}(e_1), and the fixed nonzero element of \mathbb Q_\ell(1) used to identify Tate twists with \mathbb Q_\ell. That lemma concludes that for \xi \in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) the cycle class of \mathcal O_X(1) and L = \xi \cup -, the map
   L^{\,d-n} : H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \longrightarrow H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)
 is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0 \le n \le d.

Since the class \xi of the target statement is the same cycle class of \mathcal O_X(1) (under the same identification of Tate twists), this is verbatim the desired conclusion. \hfill\blacksquare

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_q\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and use it to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). For an integer \(r\ge1\), let \(A_r\subset H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-span of the cycle classes of Cartier divisors on \(S_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\). Then the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{S_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), is semisimple on \(A_r\).
proof:
Let \(F=(\operatorname{id}_{S_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius acting on \(H^2_{\acute et}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Since \(S\) is smooth over \(\mathbb F_q\), the base change \(S_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\) is smooth. On a smooth variety every codimension-one algebraic cycle is a Cartier divisor, and every Cartier divisor is a codimension-one cycle. Hence the subspace \(A_r\) is exactly the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear span of the cycle classes \(\operatorname{cl}(z)\in H^2_{\acute et}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) of all codimension-one cycles \(z\) on \(S_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\), where the cycle classes are taken using the fixed identification \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell\).

We now apply the proved lemma \(\texttt{eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_371}\) with \(X=S\), \(j=1\), and \(m=r\). Its hypotheses are satisfied: \(q=p^a\) is a prime power, \(\ell\neq p\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and \(S\) is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_q\). The lemma states that if \(V\subset H^{2j}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-span of the cycle classes of all codimension-\(j\) cycles on \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\), then the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius satisfies \(F^m(v)=q^{mj}v\) for every \(v\in V\), and consequently \(F\) is semisimple on \(V\). Taking \(j=1\) and \(m=r\), we obtain \(F^r(v)=q^r v\) for every \(v\in A_r\), and the lemma's conclusion gives that \(F\) is semisimple on \(A_r\).

statement: Let $q=p^{a}$ be a prime power, let $\ell\neq p$ be prime, and put $k=\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q}$. Let $X$ be a proper scheme of finite type over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ admitting a finite filtration by closed subschemes $\varnothing=X_{-1}\subset X_{0}\subset\cdots\subset X_{s}=X$ such that each $U_{i}=X_{i}\setminus X_{i-1}$ is isomorphic over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ to a finite disjoint union of affine spaces over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$. For $e\ge 0$ let $n_{e}$ be the number of connected components of the strata $U_{i}$ that are isomorphic to $\mathbb{A}^{e}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}$. Then for every integer $e\ge 0$ the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $(\mathrm{id}_{X_{k}}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^{*}$, $\sigma(c)=c^{q}$, acts on $H^{2e}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{k},\mathbb{Q}_{\ell})$ with characteristic polynomial $(T-q^{e})^{n_{e}}$.
proof:
We prove the statement by induction on the index $i$ of the members $X_i$ of the filtration, applying the one-step characteristic-polynomial lemma eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/171ce3 at each step. No canonical classes attached to individual cells are constructed; only the size of the cohomology groups and the Frobenius action on them are needed.

=== Notation ===
Write $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, and for an $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $Z$ write $Z_k = Z\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec} k$. The given filtration is $\varnothing = X_{-1}\subset X_0\subset\cdots\subset X_s = X$ by closed subschemes, with $U_i := X_i\setminus X_{i-1}$ isomorphic over $\mathbb F_q$ to a finite disjoint union of affine spaces over $\mathbb F_q$. For $0\le i\le s$ and $e\ge 0$, let $n_e(i)$ denote the number of connected components of $U_i$ that are isomorphic to $\mathbb A^e_{\mathbb F_q}$, and put
\[
 m_e(i):=\sum_{j=0}^{i-1} n_e(j)
\]
(the number of $e$-cells lying in the strata strictly before $U_i$; in particular $m_e(0)=0$). By definition of the $n_e$ in the statement of the lemma, $n_e = \sum_{j=0}^{s} n_e(j) = m_e(s+1)$, so $n_e = m_e(s)$ for $s\ge 0$ with the convention that the sum for $m_e(s)$ runs over $j=0,\dots,s-1$; to avoid ambiguity we simply note that $m_e(s+1)=n_e$, and we will in fact prove for each $i\ge 0$ the statement $S(i)$: "the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius acts on $H^{2e}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_i)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ with characteristic polynomial $(T-q^e)^{m_e(i+1)}$". Then $S(s)$ is exactly the required conclusion since $m_e(s+1)=n_e$.

=== Step 1: each $X_i$ is proper of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$, and each inclusions is closed ===
$X$ is proper and of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$ by hypothesis. Each $X_i$ is a closed subscheme of $X$ (the filtration is by closed subschemes of $X$), so $X_i\to X$ is a closed immersion, hence proper and of finite type; composing with the proper (resp. finite type) morphism $X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$ shows $X_i$ is proper and of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$. Likewise $X_{i-1}\hookrightarrow X_i$ is a closed immersion, with open complement $U_i$. Finally $X_{-1}=\varnothing$ is proper of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$ and is a closed subscheme of $X_0$ (the empty subscheme is defined by the unit ideal), with open complement $U_0 = X_0$.

=== Step 2: compactly supported cohomology of the strata ===
Fix $i\ge 0$. Since $U_i\cong\bigsqcup_{\alpha=1}^{t_i}\mathbb A^{r_\alpha}_{\mathbb F_q}$ over $\mathbb F_q$ for some $t_i\ge 0$ and $r_\alpha\ge 0$, base change gives $(U_i)_k\cong\bigsqcup_{\alpha=1}^{t_i}\mathbb A^{r_\alpha}_k$, and each summand is open-and-closed in $(U_i)_k$. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/... (namely Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum) inductively on the number of summands (for $t_i=0$ the scheme is empty and $H^n_c(\varnothing,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$) yields canonical isomorphisms
\[
 H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}((U_i)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{\alpha=1}^{t_i} H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(\mathbb A^{r_\alpha}_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).
\]
By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_hc_affine_space, $H^n_c(\mathbb A^{r}_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for $n\ne 2r$ and is $1$-dimensional for $n=2r$. Hence $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}((U_i)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ for every $n$, is $0$ for $n$ odd, and
\[
 \dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell} H^{2e}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}((U_i)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) = n_e(i)\qquad\text{for every } e\ge 0.
\]

=== Step 3: finite dimensionality of $H^n((X_i)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for all $i,n$ ===
We argue by induction on $i\ge -1$. For $i=-1$ the space $(X_{-1})_k=\varnothing$ has trivial cohomology in every degree, so the claim holds.

Inductive step: assume every $H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_{i-1})_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite dimensional. The schemes $(X_i)_k$ and $(X_{i-1})_k$ are of finite type over the algebraically closed field $k$ (Step 1), and $(X_{i-1})_k\hookrightarrow (X_i)_k$ is a closed immersion with open complement $(U_i)_k$. Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_localization_les_finite_type therefore supplies a long exact sequence
\[
\cdots\to H^{n-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_{i-1})_k)\to H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}((U_i)_k)\to H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_i)_k)\to H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_{i-1})_k)\to H^{n+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}((U_i)_k)\to\cdots .
\]
Set $Q^n:=\operatorname{coker}\bigl(H^{n-1}((X_{i-1})_k)\to H^n_c((U_i)_k)\bigr)$ and $K^n:=\ker\bigl(H^n((X_{i-1})_k)\to H^{n+1}_c((U_i)_k)\bigr)$. By Step 2 and the inductive hypothesis, $Q^n$ is a quotient of a finite dimensional space and $K^n$ a subspace of a finite dimensional space, so both are finite dimensional. Exactness of the displayed sequence gives a short exact sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow Q^n\longrightarrow H^n((X_i)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow K^n\longrightarrow 0,
\]
whence $H^n((X_i)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite dimensional for every $n$. This completes the induction. (For $i=0$ this reads, with $X_{-1}=\varnothing$, that $H^n((X_0)_k)\cong H^n_c((U_0)_k)$, which Step 2 shows to be finite dimensional; the general argument above already covers it.)

Consequently, for every $i$ and $e$ the group $H^{2e}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_i)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is a finite dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space, so the characteristic polynomial of any endomorphism of it is defined.

=== Step 4: vanishing of the odd cohomology of every $X_i$ ===
For each $i\ge -1$ the truncated chain $\varnothing=X_{-1}\subset X_0\subset\cdots\subset X_i$ is a finite filtration of $X_i$ by closed $\mathbb F_q$-subschemes whose successive open complements $U_0,\dots,U_i$ are, by hypothesis, finite disjoint unions of affine spaces over $\mathbb F_q$; and $X_i$ is proper over $\mathbb F_q$ by Step 1. Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_549a applies and gives
\[
 H^{2r+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_i)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\qquad\text{for all }r\ge 0,\ \text{all } i\ge -1
\]
(for $i=-1$ this is the trivial vanishing for $\varnothing$, so no input is needed).

=== Step 5: the induction for the characteristic polynomials ===
We prove $S(i)$ for all $i\ge 0$ by induction on $i$. Fix $e\ge 0$ (equivalently, we treat all $r\ge0$ simultaneously).

Base case $i=0$: apply eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/171ce3 with $Q:=q$, $X:=X_0$, $Y:=X_{-1}=\varnothing$, $U:=U_0=X_0$. Its hypotheses are:
- $X_0$ is a proper $\mathbb F_q$-scheme and $\varnothing\subset X_0$ a closed subscheme whose open complement $U_0$ is a finite disjoint union of affine spaces: Steps 1 and the hypothesis of the lemma.
- For every $r\ge0$, $H^{2r}((X_0)_k)$ and $H^{2r}(\varnothing_k)$ are finite dimensional: Step 3 (and $H^{2r}(\varnothing)=0$).
- $H^{2r+1}(\varnothing_k)=0$: trivial.
- The $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius on $H^{2r}(\varnothing_k)=0$ has characteristic polynomial $P_r(T)=1=(T-q^r)^{0}=(T-q^r)^{m_r(0)}$, the characteristic polynomial of the zero endomorphism of the zero space.
The conclusion of 171ce3 is that the Frobenius on $H^{2r}((X_0)_k)$ has characteristic polynomial $P_r(T)(T-q^r)^{n_r(0)}=(T-q^r)^{n_r(0)}=(T-q^r)^{m_r(1)}$, which is $S(0)$.

Inductive step $i-1\to i$ with $i\ge 1$: assume $S(i-1)$, i.e. the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius on $H^{2r}((X_{i-1})_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ has characteristic polynomial $P_r(T)=(T-q^r)^{m_r(i)}$ for every $r\ge0$. Apply eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/171ce3 with $Q:=q$, $X:=X_i$, $Y:=X_{i-1}$, $U:=U_i$. Its hypotheses are:
- $X_i$ proper over $\mathbb F_q$, $X_{i-1}\subset X_i$ closed, $U_i=X_i\setminus X_{i-1}$ a finite disjoint union of affine spaces over $\mathbb F_q$: Step 1 and the hypothesis of the lemma.
- Finite dimensionality of $H^{2r}((X_i)_k)$ and $H^{2r}((X_{i-1})_k)$ for all $r$: Step 3.
- $H^{2r+1}((X_{i-1})_k)=0$ for all $r$: Step 4.
- The characteristic polynomial on $H^{2r}((X_{i-1})_k)$ is $P_r(T)$: the inductive hypothesis.
The conclusion is that the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius on $H^{2r}((X_i)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ has characteristic polynomial
\[
 P_r(T)\,(T-q^r)^{n_r(i)}=(T-q^r)^{m_r(i)+n_r(i)}=(T-q^r)^{m_r(i+1)},
\]
the last equality being the definition $m_r(i+1)=\sum_{j=0}^{i}n_r(j)$. This is $S(i)$, and it holds simultaneously for every $r\ge0$. This completes the induction.

=== Step 6: conclusion ===
Taking $i=s$ in $S(i)$, and using $X_s=X$ and $m_e(s+1)=\sum_{j=0}^{s}n_e(j)=n_e$, we obtain: for every integer $e\ge0$, the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, acts on the finite dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $H^{2e}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ with characteristic polynomial
\[
 (T-q^{e})^{n_e}.
\]
This is precisely the required statement. \qed

(Remarks on the argument: the only input from the localisation long exact sequence is the segment $H^{n-1}((X_{i-1})_k)\to H^n_c((U_i)_k)\to H^n((X_i)_k)\to H^n((X_{i-1})_k)\to H^{n+1}_c((U_i)_k)$, used solely to propagate finite dimensionality along the filtration; no "extension by zero" class in ordinary cohomology is attached to a non-open cell. The multiplicativity of characteristic polynomials in short exact sequences, the scalar action $q^r$ of Frobenius on $H^{2r}_c(\mathbb A^r_k)$, and the identification of the resulting polynomial are all contained in the cited lemma eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/171ce3, and the odd-degree vanishing in eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/... Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_549a; the new content here is the induction over the whole filtration.)

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(Y\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\mathcal E\) be a vector bundle of rank \(r+1\ge1\) on \(Y\), and let \(\pi:P=\mathbf P_Y(\mathcal E)\to Y\) be the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients. Suppose the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{Y_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\). Then the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).
proof:
Notation and typing of the hypotheses. Write $H^n(Z):=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for an $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $Z$ of finite type, with $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$. The conclusion of the lemma speaks of the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius acting on $H^n(P)$, i.e. of the automorphism $(\mathrm{id}_{P_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$; this operator is defined because $P=\mathbf P_Y(\mathcal E)$ is constructed from data on $Y$ over $\mathbb F_q$, so $P$ carries the corresponding $\mathbb F_q$-structure (equivalently: we read the hypothesis "$\mathcal E$ is a vector bundle on $Y$" as meaning $\mathcal E$ is defined over $\mathbb F_q$, which is the only reading under which the statement is well typed). The formation of $\mathbf P_Y(-)$ commutes with base change, so $P_k=\mathbf P_{Y_k}(\mathcal E_k)$, and $\pi$ is defined over $\mathbb F_q$. By hypothesis $Y$ is smooth projective geometrically connected of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$, and $\mathcal E$ has rank $r+1\ge 1$; then $\pi:P\to Y$ is projective, so $P$ is also smooth projective over $\mathbb F_q$, hence proper.

Step 0 (the meaning of "semisimple", and invertibility/finite-dimensionality of the operators). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5, for a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $V$ and $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, "$T$ is semisimple on $V$" is equivalent to "$T\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is diagonalizable on $V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$"; this is the notion used in the auxiliary lemmas quoted below, so no further translation is needed. Since $Y$ and $P$ are proper over $\mathbb F_q$, eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob applied to the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ (with its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure) shows that $H^n(Y)$ and $H^n(P)$ are finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces for every $n$. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a the maps $F_Y:=(\mathrm{id}_{Y_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ and $F_P:=(\mathrm{id}_{P_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphisms of these spaces (with inverses the geometric Frobenius pullbacks). Thus the hypothesis of the lemma says: for every $n\ge 0$, $F_Y\in\mathrm{GL}(H^n(Y))$ is semisimple.

Step 1 (Frobenius-equivariant projective bundle decomposition). Fix a nonzero element $\tau\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$, and let $c\in H^2(P)$ be the class characterised by $\mathrm{cl}(\mathcal O_P(1))=c\otimes\tau$ under $H^2(P)(1)\simeq H^2(P)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$, where $\mathcal O_P(1)$ is the tautological quotient line bundle. Applying Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_307 to $Y$, $\mathcal E$ and $P=\mathbf P_Y(\mathcal E)=\operatorname{Proj}(\operatorname{Sym}_{\mathcal O_Y}\mathcal E)$ (all over $\mathbb F_q$, with $\ell\ne p$), we obtain for every $n\ge 0$ a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism
\[
\Phi_n:\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}H^{n-2i}(Y)\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;H^n(P),\qquad (x_0,\dots,x_r)\longmapsto\sum_{i=0}^{r}\pi^*x_i\cup c^{\,i},
\]
with the convention $H^m(Y)=0$ for $m<0$, and this isomorphism carries the operator $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}q^{i}F_Y$ on the source onto $F_P$ on the target; i.e.
\[
\Phi_n\circ\Big(\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}q^{i}F_Y\Big)=F_P\circ\Phi_n .
\]
(Concretely, this is the identity $F_P(\pi^*x\cup c^i)=\pi^*(F_Yx)\cup (F_Pc)^i=\pi^*(F_Yx)\cup(q^ic)^i=q^i\,\pi^*(F_Yx)\cup c^i$, using that $\pi$ and $c$ are $\mathbb F_q$-rational up to the Tate twist, which is exactly the content of the equivariance supplied by lemma_307.)

Step 2 (each summand operator is semisimple). Fix $i\in\{0,\dots,r\}$ and $n\ge 0$. The space $H^{n-2i}(Y)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ (Step 0, and it is $0$ when $n-2i<0$, in which case there is nothing to prove), and $F_Y$ restricts to a semisimple automorphism of it by the hypothesis of the lemma (applied to the degree $n-2i\ge 0$). The scalar $q^i$ is a positive rational number, hence an element of $\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$, and $q^iF_Y$ is an invertible $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operator on $H^{n-2i}(Y)$. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_248 (semisimplicity is unchanged under multiplication by a scalar of $\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$), $q^iF_Y$ is semisimple on $H^{n-2i}(Y)$.

Step 3 (the direct sum is semisimple). The source $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}H^{n-2i}(Y)$ is a finite direct sum of finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, and $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}q^{i}F_Y$ is a direct sum of invertible operators, each semisimple by Step 2. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9 (a direct-sum operator is semisimple if and only if each summand operator is), $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}q^{i}F_Y$ is semisimple on $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}H^{n-2i}(Y)$.

Step 4 (transport across $\Phi_n$). The isomorphism $\Phi_n$ intertwines $\bigoplus_i q^iF_Y$ with $F_P$ (Step 1), both spaces being finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ and both operators invertible. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8, semisimplicity is invariant under such an intertwining isomorphism; hence $F_P$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

Step 5 (conclusion). Step 4 holds for every integer $n\ge 0$, which is precisely the required conclusion: the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $(\mathrm{id}_{P_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for all $n\ge 0$. By Step 0 (eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5) this is the same as diagonalisability after extending scalars to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. $\blacksquare$
